newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Australian ministers begin Indonesian trade push.
newsitem.headline: Australian ministers begin Indonesian trade push.

text.p: Australia has set a ministerial record in Indonesia with six ministers visiting the country at the same time as Canberra looks to strengthen investment ties with Jakarta, Trade Minister Tim Fischer said on Thursday.

The six ministers, covering the portfolios of trade, foreign affairs, industry, transport, health and environment are in Jakarta for a two-day annual Australia-Indonesia ministerial forum to boost economic and trade ties.
A seventh, the minister for education, left on Wednesday after a three-day visit, a day before the forum got under way.
"It is an all-time record for a joint ministerial (meeting) and it just shows, despite what anyone else might be saying back in Australia...its full steam ahead," Fischer told reporters.
"I don't care for the Guinness Book of Records but what I do care for is increasing (two-way) investment, trade and tourism," Fischer, who is also deputy prime minister, said.

The conservative Australian government, elected last March, had been attacked by political opponents for not placing the same emphasis on Australia's relations with its Asian neighbours as its predecessor.
The ministers will either sign or witness the signing of seven memorandums of understanding or cooperation agreements during the two-day forum.

Fischer said the forum would "add a great deal of cement to the bilateral relationship between Australia and Indonesia" as well as sort out thornier areas such as market access and anti-dumping procedures.

"It is a logical follow through of the successful prime ministerial visit last month. It is putting into action our rhetoric which is to make Asia our top trade and foreign affairs policy priority," Fischer said.

While trade has been steadily growing in recent years, Australia-Indonesia political ties have often been tense culminating with a diplomatic dispute in 1995-96 when both countries rejected ambassadors nominated by the other.
Indonesia has been angered by Australian-based vocal human rights groups and their criticisms of Jakarta's policies, particularly towards the former Portuguese colony of East Timor.
At the last forum held in Canberra, Jakarta asked Australia to control these groups which it said were harassing Indonesian diplomats based in Australia.
